transcript.content: Hi, I’m glad you came in today. What has been bothering you or bringing you in?
My doctors keep telling me I’m too thin and need to eat more, but I honestly don’t see what the fuss is about. I feel like I’m just being disciplined and careful with my health.
Are you intentionally restricting how much you eat because you’re afraid of gaining weight or becoming fat, or do you feel your body is still too big even though others say you’re underweight?

I do stick to "safe" foods because the thought of gaining weight or eating rich things makes me anxious about clogging my arteries. When I look in the mirror, I don't see myself as too thin; I just see soft spots around my belly that I still need to trim down. To me, keeping this weight off is just a matter of healthy discipline, not a problem.

Have you had any physical changes from your low weight, like your periods stopping, feeling faint, or getting very cold—and even with those problems, would gaining weight still feel unacceptable to you?

Well, at my age and being a man, things like periods don't apply, but I have to admit I've been feeling very drained lately and struggle to keep up with the house chores and my wife's appointments. Even with that fatigue, gaining weight is completely unacceptable to me because I feel like it would mean losing control, clogging my arteries, and ruining my health.

Do you spend a lot of time worrying that your body or certain parts of it are too fat, even when other people say you are very thin? Or is your eating mainly limited because you believe many foods are unhealthy or dangerous for your body?

Yes, when I look in the mirror I don't see "too thin"—I just see soft spots around my belly that I still need to trim down to protect my heart. It's also true that I highly restrict my eating because I fear certain foods; just thinking about having butter or ice cream makes my chest tight with anxiety about clogged arteries.

opening_question.question: Hi, I’m glad you came in today. What has been bothering you or bringing you in?

final_diagnosis.reason: The interview supports anorexia nervosa: the patient is described by others/doctors as markedly underweight, intentionally restricts intake, has intense anxiety about weight gain, views gaining weight as unacceptable, and shows persistent body-image distortion/lack of recognition of the seriousness of low weight. Fatigue and reduced ability to manage chores indicate medical/functional impact from low weight.
